So there’s no shame in failing, if you fail fast enough, in SaaS and Cloud.  But sometimes … well, sometimes it can hurt even worse when something great doesn’t quite work out.  When you sell instead of being able to build something epic.
I’ve tried to do my best over the years to support founders I believe in, who haven’t made it yet, by writing them checks.  It hasn’t always worked out — they didn’t make it big enough to return much of their investment, or in some cases, any money back.  Or in one case, they were later shut down due to regulatory issues (a bummer).
But what hurts me most isn’t losing the money itself.  It’s when something could have been truly amazing.  And then it wasn’t.  That’s the worst part.
One recent example I’m still thinking about is Brex.
What happened?
Well, it seemed like magic at first.  A new type of corporate card, built right after Stripe launched.  The cards were super easy to use, and had tons of functionality and security built-in that the incumbents simply couldn’t match.  CEO Henrique Dubugras was incredibly charismatic, and somehow got the company off to an incredible start.
Fast forward to today, though, things aren’t quite working out:
It raised at a stunning $12.3 Billion valuation,
And sold for $5.2 Billion (!)
Yes, it lost almost half of its market cap.  That’s hard to see.
And here’s the thing … this makes sense
.  They’ve now crossed $800m in ARR!  So how did they lose half their market cap?  Well, in fact, it’s simple math.
They’re worth roughly 7–8x ARR these days.  Just a smidge above average, and actually below where they started.
The real problem is they took too long to get past $700m-$800m in ARR.  Because during that time, their burn rate stayed high.  You need to keep the machine going.  If you don’t, you never really get anywhere.

So I've talked on SaaStr for years now about hiring a great VP of Sales. How to hire one. What mistakes you make when you don't hire a good enough one. And what happens with a mediocre VP of Sales versus a very strong one. But two related questions have come up again recently on our social media channels on X and LinkedIn that I wanted to update everyone on. So first, does a great VP of Sales need to bring in a bunch of managers under them right off the bat? And second, how much can you criticize a VP of Sales if they're just doing worse than you expected?
So the answer to the first part of this is yes, a great VP of Sales will almost always want to bring in their own team underneath her. They'll almost all do that. Now some VPs of Sales will try to start off without any direct reports, especially those that haven't done this before. Some will be happy to work directly with the existing reps and maybe even take over managing an individual rep or two themselves. But most seasoned VPs of Sales will quickly want to bring in 2-3 directors underneath them, sometimes more. The best ones won't wait long. If you see someone bringing in lots of managers early, that could well be a sign she knows how to scale. But here's my advice: let them build the team they think they need. It often doesn't really matter which exact folks you hire yourself in the end. You might like some of these hires. Maybe you wouldn't hire half of them yourself. But so long as they're growing revenue, leave them alone. Even if you aren't sure why they made each hire. My second point was something a lot of founders struggle with: is it OK to criticize your VP of Sales when things aren't going well? In fact, I'd argue no. At least not unless you know you're firing them.

Anneka Gupta
AI will also have an impact on how we think about personalization. It used to take weeks to get your first lead back when you launched a new feature, now you can do it in hours and days, which makes it more practical. We’re going to start looking at this differently. But I don’t know if we’ll end up there. That being said, AI is part of it, platforms are part of it. And promises are part of it. The promises around what customers expect for AI capabilities. A lot of these things are aspirational. But they’re good to talk about because they help us set goals for our companies. What should we be doing next year versus what should we be trying out next year? Some of these features aren’t even possible yet. There are some cool use cases where you can tell AI to build a report based on a bunch of data and it builds something pretty nice. You asked me three questions. One, will people buy more products per company? Two, will NRR come down as you scale? Three, will driving up ACVs drive acceleration? My answer to number one is yes. In my previous life, I sold a very verticalized solution to retailers. It did very well. But they would never buy another product from anyone else.

traces.answer: So I did want to step back on this because one thing we know is almost everyone in B2B software now wants to use AI to personalize the customer experience more than ever before. We talked to an incredible CMO recently who literally just left her job, she'd been running marketing at a very successful unicorn for years. She came out swinging in our podcast like she hasn't seen anything better than ChatGPT for personalization. That's how excited she is. But what does that really mean? Is every single interaction with your product going to have to be personalized? Can they all be done through a chatbot and a prompt? A lot of folks think so. So I wanted to see if I could find where this first originated. It seems like such a great idea. Everyone loves personalization. They're good at it when they have lots of humans and can do it manually, but even there, customers complain they don't get enough attention. What would happen if we could magically deliver that to each and every customer, no matter how small, no matter how large, with a prompt? The originator here I believe was the founder of Rippling, Parker Conrad. He wrote a pretty interesting article on his thoughts on the future of enterprise SaaS after attending SaaStr Annual. He gave us some great content. He had some great insights. One of them was, "I've decided the future of business software is to make it hyper-personalized." Now, I'm sure many of you love the word "hyperpersonalized" because it sounds cool. But actually, it's probably already been achieved by many of your competitors. Rippling's vision here is that AI will allow companies to build exactly what customers want -- customized workflows, tailored experiences, and automated processes all without needing to code.
